messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
The lines do not show Majeed as openly malicious, but they do not erase his cunning or apathy either. His command — “Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village” — has a practical, almost mechanical clarity. He does not ask permission, explain the danger, or reassure the women; Rahima is simply described as “bewildered” and at his heels. Jamila, too, is not shown choosing to go; she is carried, “wrapped in a thin... quilt.” That image can look protective, but it also reduces her to a body he transports. So the same traits are present, though in a subtler form: his cunning appears as fast, economical decision-making, while his apathy appears as emotional distance and a refusal to fully attend to their feelings.

As for motive, the better reading is **teleological** rather than **deontological**. A deontological reading would require that he acts because saving them is right in itself, or because he is moved by pure good-will, duty, or conscience. The excerpt does not foreground moral certainty, compassion, or guilt. It foregrounds movement, direction, and outcome: he takes them to the village, he carries Jamila, he leads Rahima. Given his earlier portrayal as cunning and apathetic, his action reads less like selfless rescue and more like strategic management of a crisis. Even if the village is safer, the moment suggests that he is arranging a useful consequence — keeping them alive, keeping them under control, or preserving his own position. The detail that “the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him” reinforces this: he is reacting under pressure, not acting from serene moral principle.

Thus, the passage can be read as a temporary mask of care over an underlying pattern of calculation. It does not prove that he has become genuinely selfless; it shows that a cunning, self-protective mind can also produce actions that look like rescue.

The required single-word palindromes are: level, madam, civic, tenet, refer, radar, rotor, rotator, reviver, redder.
